strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated hybrid Gaussian-particle framework that couples MPM physical simulation with 3D Gaussian Splatting to add dynamic global weather effects (snow, rain, fog, sandstorm) as well as falling/landing rigid objects to static reconstructed scenes.

The three-stage pipeline (Gaussian-to-particle mapping, MPM simulation with a mesh-derived static particle set, particle-to-Gaussian re-rendering with effect-specific appearance and collision handling) is a sensible and technically coherent design that allows dynamic elements to interact with existing scene geometry, addressing a real limitation of prior single-object physics-based Gaussian animation and of purely static weather-compositing methods (e.g., ClimateNeRF).

Effect-specific collision handling (surface projection for snow/sand, a volumetric wetness grid with temporal decay for rain) is a concrete and demonstrated technical contribution, supported by a clear ablation (Figure 7) showing qualitative benefit versus a no-collision-handling variant.

Reasonably broad qualitative demonstration across five scenes (Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks & Temples) and multiple effect types, plus extension to object-level dynamics (falling leaves/feathers, landing drone/bee), and a controllability study (Figure 4) showing tunable fog color, sand scale, and snow quantity.

Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix specifying MPM material parameters, grid resolution, particle emission rates, rendering scale/opacity/color settings per effect, and links/settings for baseline reproduction.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparisons (Table 1) are against static 3D editing methods (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) that are not designed to produce dynamic, temporally evolving effects; this is an inherently favorable and somewhat unfair comparison for demonstrating 'state-of-the-art' dynamic weather synthesis, since the baselines cannot represent motion at all. No quantitative comparison is made against more directly relevant dynamic/physics-based methods mentioned in related work (e.g., PhysGaussian, Gaussian Splashing, or the concurrent RainyGS), even though RainyGS is explicitly acknowledged as tackling the same rain-effect problem.

The evaluation metrics used (CLIP similarity, CLIP direction similarity, VQAScore) are single-frame, semantic/text-alignment proxies borrowed from text-guided editing evaluation; they do not directly measure temporal coherence, physical plausibility of motion, or realism of dynamics, which are the paper's central claims ('physically plausible motion', 'significantly outperforms ... in physical realism'). No physics-grounded metric, temporal-consistency metric (e.g., optical-flow or video-based FVD), or user study is provided to substantiate these claims.

Evaluation breadth is limited to five scenes total and effects are demonstrated mostly qualitatively (Figures 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10); there is no systematic per-effect quantitative table across all five scenes, and only one ablation figure (qualitative, no numeric ablation metrics) is given for collision handling.

Interaction is explicitly one-directional: dynamic particles react to the static scene, but the static scene cannot be deformed or moved by the dynamic effects, which the authors acknowledge but which limits the realism of e.g. heavy sandstorm or debris interactions.

Appearance parameters are largely hand-tuned per effect and per scene (extensive manually chosen scale/opacity/color/velocity constants listed in the appendix), raising concerns about generalization to new scenes/effects without significant manual re-tuning, which the authors themselves list as a limitation.

Runtime is reported only as a single aggregate number (7 FPS on an RTX A5000) without characterizing how it scales with particle count, effect type, or scene complexity, leaving practical usability and scalability to more particles/longer sequences unclear.

Mesh extraction and the reliance on TSDF fusion for collision geometry could introduce failure modes in thin or complex structures (e.g., foliage, bicycles) that are not explicitly analyzed; the paper does not discuss failure cases or robustness limits of the mesh-based collision approach.
